text.p: Bernard Tapie, bankrupt former tycoon, French politician and soccer boss, entered La Sante prison in central Paris on Monday evening for the first of what may be many nights in jail, his lawyer said.
"He has just entered prison," attorney Jean-Yves Lienard told Reuters.

The former cabinet minister, who has expressed terror at the prospect of going to jail, had spent the weekend pondering last-ditch ways of avoiding going behind bars but in the end concluded it was the appropriate thing to do, Lienard said.
He was required by law to report to prison on the eve of the hearing on his appeal against an eight-month sentence for rigging a soccer match. Otherwise the appeal would have been scrapped.
Lienard earlier had visited the jail to discuss the conditions of his client's incarceration. "He won't come unless they give it a fresh coat of paint," the lawyer had joked.

French news media said Tapie, 54, had wanted to know in particular whether he would be allowed to use his portable telephone in prison -- the answer was 'No' -- and how many showers a day he would be allowed.

He was also reported to have called Loik Le Floch Prigent, the former chairman of state railways and of oil giant Elf Aquitaine, recently released from six months in pre-trial detention, to inquire about conditions at La Sante.
VIPs in La Sante include guerrilla mastermind "Carlos" as well as Le Floch Prigent.
The Supreme Court was to rule on Tuesday on Tapie's final appeal against an eight-month sentence for bribing players to fix a soccer match between Marseille and Valenciennes in 1993.

If the court upholds the sentence, he will stay in jail and serve the rest of his term. If it quashes his conviction, then Tapie, whose business empire once included sports equipment giant Adidas, will walk free until a re-trial.
He faces a blizzard of other legal actions over his failed holding company, tax affairs and his stewardship of Marseille.
Tapie, who recently began a career as a film actor, is hoping for an open prison regime under which he could spend only his nights in jail while working as an actor during the day.

Justice sources doubted the Supreme Court would put off Tuesday's ruling because of lingering doubts about whether he was still protected from imprisonment by his membership of the European Parliament, his last political mandate.

A French court last year ruled he was ineligible for public office because he was personally bankrupt. But the Strasbourg-based parliament is not due to eject him formally until the start of its next plenary session on February 17.
Tapie was convicted of bribing Valenciennes players to lose to Marseille just days before his team played the 1993 European Cup Final. Marseille won the final against AC Milan by 1-0.
He is also appealing against a six-month conviction for tax fraud over his luxury yacht and will go on trial in May on charges of falsifying the accounts at Marseille.
